chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mada'ini, from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who has missed days from the month of Ramadan, how should he make them up? He said: If he has two days, he should break fast (skip one day) between them; and if he has five days, he should break fast between them (skip days); and he is not permitted to fast more than eight consecutive days. And if he has eight or ten days, he should break fast between them (skip one day). The meaning in this narration is that whoever is obligated to make up the month of Ramadan is not required to make them up consecutively, according to what was obligatory for him to fast initially. Thus, what this report contains regarding the command to break fast and separate between these days is merely a command of choice and permission, not obligation or recommendation, because we have clarified that making them up consecutively is superior in the first narration.

key_terms.قَضَاءُ شَهْرِ رَمَضَانَ: Making up missed fasts of Ramadan
key_terms.يُفْطِرْ بَيْنَهُمَا: Breaking fast between them (skipping a day)

ai.seo_question: How should missed Ramadan fasts be made up according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar clarifies the juristic distinction between the obligation (wajib) and recommendation (mandub) of consecutive fasting for Qada, citing Shaykh al-Tusi’s analysis that skipping days is a permissible choice rather than a strict requirement. It establishes a practical limit of eight consecutive days to prevent hardship, reflecting the Shia emphasis on ease in religious duties while maintaining the superiority of continuity. This ruling addresses the specific scenario of making up missed Ramadan fasts, distinguishing it from the general rules of fasting.
